question: “The residents should have a say in the park project.” What is the speaker asking for?
choices: Residents should be able to influence the decision.
Every resident should give a speech at the opening.
Residents should make every decision on their own.
Residents should hear the final decision first.
note: Having “a say” means having a voice in the decision. Being told the result first still leaves the choice to others.

picture.alt: A blank ballot paper and a ballot box.

question: The library asks, “Can you take on the Saturday book club?” What would saying yes involve?
choices: Running it yourself from now on.
Trying the club once as a reader.
Giving the current organiser advice.
Helping choose someone to lead it.
note: “Take on” means accept responsibility. “Sit in on” would be an invitation to observe a meeting.

picture.alt: Two closed books beside a quill.

question: “With four projects, we’re spreading ourselves too thin.” What worries the organiser?
choices: Each project gets too little of the team’s time.
All the projects attract the same volunteers.
The team travels too far between meetings.
Nobody has decided which project starts first.
note: A team spread too thin has too many commitments for its resources. Distance between sites could be a separate problem.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: The community centre suggests a “trial run” of your games afternoon. What is it agreeing to?
choices: Trying one session before deciding on more.
Offering a regular slot for the rest of the year.
Watching another centre hold the same event.
Advertising the idea to see how people respond.
note: A trial run means doing the activity on a limited basis. Advertising tests interest, while a trial tests how the session works.

picture.alt: A wooden game piece beside a die.

question: “The repair café is ready. Now we need to get the word out.” What does the group need?
choices: More local people to hear about it.
A shorter name for the project.
Someone to check the wording of the rules.
Permission to confirm a starting date.
note: “Get the word out” means spread the news. Checking the wording might be a task for whoever writes the leaflets.

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.

question: Your team wants to start a visiting scheme for older neighbours. Nobody has asked the residents what sort of visits they’d enjoy. What do you suggest first?
choices: Could we ask a few residents what would make a visit worthwhile?
Why don’t we match each resident with a volunteer this afternoon?
Shall we copy the programme that worked for families at the youth centre?
Could we book the community hall for a celebration at the end of term?
note: Talking to residents lets them shape the visits. Matching volunteers comes later, once people have chosen to take part.

question: The bike workshop needs someone there every Saturday. You can help twice a month and want to be clear before names go on the rota. What do you say?
choices: I can do the first and third Saturdays. Does that cover part of the gap?
Saturdays usually suit me. Put me down and I’ll confirm each week.
I’d be happy to help the team work out how many people it needs.
If the workshop moved to Fridays, I might be able to come every single week.
note: Naming two dates gives the organiser something reliable to plan around. “I’ll confirm each week” leaves all four dates uncertain.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: Two people have been debating a homework club for ten minutes. Ali, who volunteers at one, has been waiting to speak. You’re chairing. What do you say?
choices: Before we go on, Ali, what have you seen at your homework club?
Could the two of you sum up your positions before we carry on?
Ali works at a club, so I think we can guess which side he’s on.
Let’s put these two views to a vote while they’re fresh in our minds.
note: Asking Ali about his experience brings another voice into the decision. Summing up is useful once everyone has had a chance to speak.

question: A shop can donate notebooks but has no staff free to teach at your homework club. You need both. How do you answer?
choices: The notebooks would be welcome. We’ll keep looking for volunteer tutors.
Could you send a tutor instead? We’re trying to keep donations simple.
Could we wait and make one announcement once both needs are covered?
Thanks for the offer. We’ll get back to you once all the tutors are ready.
note: Accepting the supplies covers one need and keeps the other visible. Asking for a tutor instead would fit an offer with a choice attached.

question: For a park clean-up, residents prefer Sunday morning, but the student team can only come after lunch. What do you propose?
choices: Could residents collect in the morning and students sort the bags after lunch?
Shall we tell residents it’ll be after lunch and hope they can move things?
I suppose the students will have to miss this one if mornings are popular.
Should we ask everyone to vote between Sunday morning and Saturday morning instead?
note: Splitting the tasks keeps both groups involved. A vote between mornings would still exclude the students.

question: Your mural team has paint for one wall. A neighbour suggests painting the whole street. Everyone likes the idea, but the budget is fixed. What do you say?
choices: Let’s finish the wall we can afford and price the rest for a later stage.
If the whole street prefers that idea, let’s spread the paint across all the walls.
Before we buy more paint, shall we pick colours for every house?
We can announce the whole street today and deal with the costs later.
note: A later stage keeps the idea possible while protecting the first wall. Planning every house would fit a project with funds to cover the street.

question: The tool library lent out 90 tools this month. A councillor asks how many different households it helped. You counted loans, not borrowers. What do you say?
choices: We recorded 90 loans. I’d need borrower figures to give you a household total.
Roughly 90 households, though a few tools may have come back early.
Could I send you a report on which tools were most popular instead?
We should ask the volunteers which household borrowed the most often this month.
note: A household can borrow more than once. “Roughly 90 households” would need evidence that almost every loan went to a different one.

question: The centre can lend you its repair room only when a trained supervisor is there. One has volunteered for Tuesdays. People are asking which days are definitely available. What do you say?
choices: We can confirm Tuesdays. We’ll need another supervisor before we add a day.
We can open twice a week, provided somebody has the supervisor’s phone number.
We can run a second day if we keep the equipment cupboard locked.
Could we announce the whole week now and ask for more supervisors?
note: Tuesday meets the condition. A phone number would be enough only if the centre allowed supervision from a distance.

picture.alt: An old engine with a flywheel.

question: The team chooses an upstairs hall for a public meeting. You learn the lift will be closed that evening. Invitations haven’t gone out. What do you say?
choices: Could we look at the downstairs room before we send out the invitations?
Let’s add a note about the stairs so people know what to expect.
We can ask at the meeting whether anyone had any trouble getting up the stairs.
Could we reserve the front seats for people who arrive a little late?
note: Changing rooms can remove the barrier before anyone is invited. A note about stairs helps people plan but still leaves some unable to attend.

picture.alt: Steps and railings at an underground railway entrance.

question: Your group has agreed to run a food collection next Thursday. As everyone gets up to leave, the driver asks who will unlock the hall. Nobody knows. What do you say?
choices: Before we go, who can get the key and meet the driver on Thursday?
Let’s add the hall to the list of things to remember next time.
Could you remind us why we chose Thursday for the collection?
Great, it sounds like the plan is in place. Thanks for coming.
note: Naming a person turns an open question into a commitment. Adding it to a list helps only if someone takes responsibility for it.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.
